questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: To me, it was important to go outside of Europe and preferably to an English-speaking country. Canada has always been at the top of my travel list, and I felt like it was the perfect opportunity to go there on exchange. I chose Montreal because of the location, what I'd read about Concordia University, and because I always wanted to learn some French

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was a bit complicated. The university (and Canada in general) is not quite as technologically advanced as Denmark, so it required a lot of waiting hours at the International Students Office at uni, and going around the city to get everything in order. Also the way the university works is quite different from in Denmark. But they were extremely helpful at the offices, and a lot of the people I met in the beginning were either going through the same things in regards to arrival or had done it already, so we could help each other. But things like obtaining a student ID, metro card etcetera, was just generally more time consuming than what I was used to from Denmark. Also, finding information on Concordia University's website is not that logical.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The International Students Office were very helpful with requests, but it's not like you're offered it automatically. I did reach out to the student counsellors and whoever else I needed to talk to upon arrival.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
To me it was actually pretty easy. I made a profile on a website for people looking for a place and people who had available rooms or apartments. I was contacted by someone who had a room in a house with four other international students, and after speaking with her, she offered me the room. My experience and my understanding from friends there is that it is easier to find housing in Montreal than in Copenhagen, but not always cheaper. I got lucky and found a super cheap room, but generally, price levels are the same, or maybe a bit cheaper, than in Copenhagen. But on-campus housing is pretty expensive, so I would definitely recommend looking for an off-campus place, through Facebook or websites like
roomgo.ca
. My rent was 550 Canadian dollars per month, while on-camping housing costs 1200-1500 CAD/month.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I loved living off campus. It gave me a chance to explore much more of the city, and even though I lived in the city centre, it was great to be off campus. If you live with roommates it is an easy way to meet new people, and I really liked that not everything happened on campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The course registration really seems to me to be much more complicated than it needs to be. After your acceptance at the uni, you get a login for a MyConcordia page, where you can find and register for courses. You can read (very very short) descriptions of the courses in the course catalogue on the general website, and there it will say if there is some prerequisite to taking the course. A lot of them don't apply to exchange students though, depending on your program, but there are also more restrictions on courses that won't be stated in the course catalogue. Therefore, when you register for courses, it will sometimes tell you that it is unavailable to you, despite it not being full. Once you successfully register a Moodle page is going to become available, where you can see course materials etc.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can contact the particular departments or the International Students Office with questions. I contacted the departments quite a lot in the registration process to know why a course was unavailable to me. Sometimes, I couldn't take it because I was an exchange student, but a lot of the time it was simply because I didn't have the prerequisite normally required - but I could take it anyway. At the departments, they can either tell you why you can't register or open the registration to you. There is going to be a bit of waiting time for them to be reply though.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got some of the classes that were my first choice, but not all, because they were either full or unavailable. But in the end I wound up with some interesting classes.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Begin registering for courses early. That will give you time to sort out any registration issues, but also, many classes fill up pretty fast. So do it as early as possible.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The academic level is a lot lower than at UCPH, at least that was my experience. I found a lot of the coursework and reading to be closer to high school levels in Denmark. I also had way less readings than normally at UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: At Concordia, your grade for the course is not entirely dependent on the final exam, like it is at UCPH. It normally only counts for 20-30% of your grade. The rest will be attendance, participation, tests, midterms and papers. However, I found that the in-class teaching style, for the most part, was pretty similar to that of UCPH.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Media Criticism, Propaganda, Contemporary News Media, Introduction to Contemporary Concerns in Women's Studies.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend Media Criticism at the Communication and Journalism Institute, and Contemporary Concerns in Women's Studies at the Simone de Beauvoir Institute. Both were quite different in content than what I would have at UCPH, but in a very good way. I found them to be the most giving courses, and also the best structured ones.
I recommend avoiding the online classes. I found them to be not very well structured, with very little help available, and also not that interesting. Classes are also a good way to meet people, so I really recommend prioritizing physical classes over online ones.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I was a bit surprised that everything costs money at Concordia - like student IDs, transcripts, some paperwork etc. It's not a large amount, like $13 for student ID and around $20 for the transcript, but still, nothing is free there. Also, tips are very much expected, not just at restaurants, but also hair salons, tattoo shops etc. You are expected to pay 15-20% in tips. Taxes are never included in the price listed, but added at the counter. Taxes vary depending on the item you buy, but are around 10-15%

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Public transportation is pretty cheap for students. You can get a card for half the normal price if you are a student, where you can ride unlimited. Buying groceries was more expensive than I thought it would be, and more expensive than in Denmark. However, eating out is pretty cheap compared to the cost of food at the grocery store, and Montreal has endless amazing restaurants where you can get really good food pretty cheap.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Concordia has tons of clubs, sports, places you can volunteer, and just general activities you can participate in.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would really recommend to take part in the activities offered by the Concordia Ski & Snowboard club, and the Concordia Outdoors club. Both plan really fun events like skiing, weekend trips, hikes etc, that would be a bit hard to organize yourself and it is a great way to meet new people. I also volunteered at the student café, which was a fun way to meet new people as well.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Montreal is a really amazing, and there are tons of things to do there, like go to museums, parks, explore the different neighborhoods etc. I also really recommend getting out of the city. Canada has so much amazing nature, and it is amazing to get out of the city to ski, hike, or explore in other ways. You really only need to leave the city borders to find amazing mountains, national parks, and some other nice cities are pretty easily accessible by bus or train, like New York, Toronto, Quebec City etcetera. It is also fun to rent a car and spend a weekend at a cabin.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I actually found it to be easier than I was expecting. Of course it is a challenge to move to a new country, and I'd never been to Canada before my exchange, so I didn't really know what to expect. But culturally, it was not that far away from other cultures I've seen or like the Danish culture.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I actually mostly made friends with international students, but the local students I did make friends with were my roommates, and ones I met through activities at the university, like clubs and volunteering. Canadians are extremely friendly and chatty, so they are pretty open to new people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I found the Canadian French pretty difficult, but it is absolutely not necessary to know French in Montreal, as everyone is at least bilingual. One of the things I found it hardest to adjust to was the climate, which has way colder, way more extreme weather than in Denmark. The winter lasts from October to April, and can have extreme temperatures and other weather occurrences I had never seen. But it was also very interesting living in that sort of climate.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really appreciated how multicultural Montreal and Canada in general is. There are lots of people from all over the world there, and it is so interesting to meet people from so many different places. I also really appreciated how open, friendly and spontaneous people are there.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: I would say that one of the best things Montreal has to offer in my opinion is the mix of cultures, so be sure to explore that. But also get out of the city to see some other parts of the country, which looks nothing like Denmark, and has so much to offer. It is a good idea to think in advance what you would want out of your stay, and what the best scenario would be, and then go for that - whether it is pursuing academic challenges, making a lot of friends, trying a lot of new things etcetera. But I will also say that, to me at least, my stay was nothing like I imagined it.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Concordia offers language courses for international students (they don't give credit or is an actual university class). I'd recommend avoiding those, as they are pretty poorly organized and you don't get very much out of it.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: My new friends. I was very worried about how hard it would be to make new friends, but I found it pretty easy, as particularly international students are all in the same boat regarding the fact that they don't know anyone or anything there, and all just want to make the most of it.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I actually found the time difference to Denmark pretty challenging, which was a bit surprising. But I also found it challenging to work out the university systems and figuring out how everything worked.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
